orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling Lockwood the story. It picks up straight after old Mr. Earnshaw's death at the end of Chapter V, so scholars date it to late 1777. Catherine is about twelve.

notes.g: Hindley Earnshaw, Catherine's older brother.
notes.n: His father sent him away to college in Chapter V. Now, with his father dead, he is master of Wuthering Heights.

notes.t: set the neighbours gossiping right and left
notes.g: Got people talking all over the neighbourhood.

notes.t: he brought a wife with him
notes.g: This is Frances, the wife Catherine's diary mentions in Chapter III.
notes.n: Nelly doesn't name her in this chapter, but the diary did.

notes.t: neither money nor name to recommend her
notes.g: No fortune and no respectable family to make her a good match.
notes.n: Families who owned land expected a son's bride to bring money or good connections. That is probably why Hindley kept the marriage secret.

notes.t: kept the union from his father
notes.g: Kept the marriage secret from his father.
By herself; through her own doings.
The doorway; the entrance of a house.
Half-witted; a bit simple in the head.
notes.m: 'Silly' could mean feeble-minded or simple, harsher than today's 'goofy'.

notes.g: Bedroom.
Getting Catherine and Heathcliff dressed (for the funeral).
Wild, uncontrolled feeling.
Seeing everyone dressed in black for mourning.
notes.n: After a death, the family, servants and mourners wore black, sometimes for a year.

notes.g: Jumped with fright and shook.
notes.m: 'Start' here means to flinch or jump suddenly, not to begin.

notes.g: Began to cry.
With healthy, rosy skin.

notes.t: set her all in a quiver
notes.g: Made her tremble all over.
In a worrying, nagging way.
What these signs were a warning of.
notes.n: Nelly, telling the story years later, hints that the breathlessness and the cough meant something. Keep them in mind.

notes.g: Felt no urge to pity her.
Outsiders; people not from round here.
notes.m: Not necessarily people from another country. To Yorkshire villagers, anyone from another district was a 'foreigner'.

notes.g: Hindley (not his dead father).
Become thinner.
Grown pale.
From then on.
Live and sit in the back kitchen, the working room behind the main kitchen.
notes.n: Until now the servants sat with the family (Chapter V). Hindley pushes them out to show he is the master now.

notes.g: Leave the main living room ('the house') to him and his wife.
notes.n: Remember that the big family room at the Heights is called 'the house' (Chapter I).

notes.g: A small private sitting room.
notes.n: Genteel homes had parlours. Hindley has come back from the south with refined ideas, and wants one instead of the old farmhouse living room.

notes.g: The stone floor, scrubbed until it was pale.
Plates of pewter, a dull grey metal made mostly of tin.
notes.n: Lockwood saw 'ranks of immense pewter dishes' shining here in Chapter I.

notes.g: Shelves or a dresser for showing off glazed pottery.
notes.n: 'Delf' is pottery named after Delft in Holland, famous for its blue-and-white ware.

notes.g: A place for the dogs to lie, probably the arch under the dresser Lockwood saw in Chapter I.
Chattered in a childish way.
Irritable and whiny.
Cruel and bossy, like a tyrant.
Showing.

notes.t: deprived him of the instructions of the curate
notes.g: Stopped his lessons with the local curate.
notes.n: The curate taught the children (Chapter V). Catherine's diary in Chapter III shows this new regime: Hindley swore he would 'reduce him to his right place'.

notes.g: Do farm work outside, like a hired hand.
Put up with being pushed down in rank.
notes.n: Heathcliff has gone from the old master's favourite to a farm servant.

notes.g: Looked very likely.
As rough and uncivilised as wild people.
notes.m: 'Rude' meant rough, untaught and unpolished, not just impolite.

notes.g: Careless; not paying attention.

notes.t: seen after their going to church
notes.g: Made sure they went to church.
Scolded him for his carelessness.
Stayed away.
A beating with a whip, strap or stick.

notes.t: a fast from dinner or supper
notes.g: Having to go without her midday meal or her evening meal.
notes.m: 'Dinner' was the main meal at midday; 'supper' was the lighter evening meal.

notes.g: The high, open, wild land of heather and rough grass around the Heights.
The punishment that came afterwards.

notes.t: set as many chapters as he pleased for Catherine to get by heart
notes.g: Give Catherine as many Bible chapters as he liked to learn by heart.
notes.n: Memorising Scripture was both a lesson and a punishment for children.

notes.g: Worked out; schemed up.
Wicked; bad.
notes.m: Stronger then than today's mild word for a misbehaving child.

notes.g: The poor children, who had nobody to stand up for them.
It happened.
Sent out of the sitting room as a punishment.
In a rage.
notes.m: 'Passion' here means anger, not love or enthusiasm.

notes.g: Lock the doors with their sliding bars.
My window.
notes.n: A lattice window has small panes of glass set in a crisscross frame of lead.

notes.g: Listen.
The order forbidding it.
I made out the sound of footsteps.
notes.m: 'Distinguish' here means to pick out with the senses, not to make famous.

notes.g: Now this means Hindley.
notes.n: Since his father's death, Hindley is 'Mr. Earnshaw' and 'the master'.

notes.g: You'll be in trouble.
Thrown out; dismissed from the house.
The Lintons' house in the valley, where Lockwood is now living.
notes.n: It is about four miles from the Heights by road (Chapter II).

notes.g: A free wander, with nobody watching.
The family at Thrushcross Grange: Mr. and Mrs. Linton and their two children.
notes.n: Nelly first mentioned 'the little Lintons' in Chapter V.

notes.t: burning their eyes out before the fire
notes.g: Staring into the warm fire for hours.
Drilled in religious questions and answers.
notes.n: A catechism is a fixed set of questions and answers about Christian belief, learned by heart. Heathcliff is describing Joseph's Sunday treatment of them.

notes.g: A list of names from the Bible to memorise.
Don't preach at me, Nelly.
notes.n: 'Cant' is pious, moralising talk that sounds insincere.

notes.g: The private grounds around the Grange (Thrushcross Park, Chapter III).
Wet, spongy, muddy ground on the moor.
A flower bed.
The best room, used for receiving guests.
notes.n: Short for 'withdrawing room'. The Heights has nothing like it.

notes.g: From there.
Wooden panels closed over windows at night.
Standing on the ledge at the foot of the wall.
notes.m: Not an underground floor. Here the 'basement' is the projecting base of the house wall.

notes.t: a shower of glass-drops hanging in silver chains
notes.g: A chandelier hung with glass crystals.
notes.n: A sign of great wealth to the two children from the farmhouse.

notes.g: Thin candles.
The parents, owners of Thrushcross Grange.
Edgar Linton and Isabella, the two Linton children.
Isabella Linton, Edgar's younger sister, about eleven.

notes.t: as if witches were running red-hot needles into her
notes.g: As if she were being tortured.
notes.n: People believed witches tormented their victims with pins and needles.

notes.g: The stone floor in front of the fireplace.
Blaming each other.
Openly and loudly.
Spoiled creatures.
My situation here at the Heights.
The triangular top of a house's end wall, under the roof.
All together, at the same moment.
Pulling back the iron bars that bolted the door.
A big, fierce guard dog.
notes.n: Bulldogs then were tall, powerful dogs bred for bull-baiting and guarding, not today's squat pets.

notes.g: Disgusting; hateful.
Stuck through on the horns, like meat on a roasting spit.
Shouted loudly.
Destroy any devil in the Christian world.
Hold on tight, Skulker!
notes.n: Skulker is the Lintons' bulldog. A 'skulker' is someone who lurks in hiding.

notes.g: What Skulker had caught; his prey.
Choked until it let go.
Hanging, drooping lips.
Drool; saliva.
Curses.
One of the Lintons' servants.
Old Mr. Linton, the children's father, shouted from the doorway.
notes.n: In this chapter 'Linton' on its own means the father.

notes.g: A real bad lot; a thorough villain.

notes.t: Very like the robbers were for putting them through the window
notes.g: Very likely the robbers meant to push them in through the window.
notes.n: Robert imagines the children are part of a gang of burglars.

notes.g: The wooden frame for hanging criminals.
notes.n: In the 1770s, burglary could be punished by hanging.

notes.g: Put your gun down.
The day his tenants paid their rent, so there was cash in the house.
notes.n: Mr. Linton is a landlord who lets farms to tenant farmers.

notes.g: Give them a 'welcome' (meant as a threat).

notes.t: To beard a magistrate in his stronghold
notes.g: To defy a magistrate in his own home.
notes.n: Mr. Linton is a magistrate (a justice of the peace), a local gentleman who judged minor crimes. To 'beard' someone is to confront them boldly.

notes.g: Sunday, the holy day of rest.
Rude, disrespectful boldness.
Mrs. Linton, his wife.
It is only a boy.

notes.t: before he shows his nature in acts as well as features
notes.g: Before he acts as wickedly as his face suggests.
notes.n: Many people then believed you could read a person's character in their face.

notes.g: Glasses.
Speaking in a babyish way, saying 'th' for 's'.

notes.t: the son of the fortune-teller that stole my tame pheasant
notes.g: Isabella thinks Heathcliff looks like a Gypsy boy.
notes.n: Travelling Romani people were known for fortune-telling, and were often unfairly blamed for thefts.

notes.g: Came back to consciousness.
Curious.
Gathered enough sense.
Both families go to the same church in Gimmerton.
notes.n: Church was where gentry families saw their neighbours.

notes.g: That's Catherine Earnshaw.
notes.n: 'Miss Earnshaw' was the polite title for the eldest daughter of the family. Being a gentleman's daughter changes how the Lintons treat her.

notes.g: The lady: Mrs. Linton.
Roaming wildly about the countryside.
An old, now offensive word for a Romani person.
notes.n: Mrs. Linton judges Heathcliff by his dark looks, as Mrs. Earnshaw did ('gipsy brat') in Chapter IV.

notes.g: Dressed in black because a close relative has died.
notes.n: Catherine's father died only weeks ago.

notes.g: Crippled permanently.
Blameworthy.
The name of the curate, as Nelly explains.
Complete ignorance of religion, like a pagan.

notes.t: that strange acquisition my late neighbour made
notes.g: That odd thing my dead neighbour (old Mr. Earnshaw) picked up.
notes.n: Everyone round about knows the story of the boy brought home from Liverpool (Chapter IV).

notes.g: A sailor from India or South Asia working on a European ship.
notes.n: Ports like Liverpool had many. Mr. Linton is only guessing at where Heathcliff came from, from his dark looks.

notes.g: An abandoned child from the Americas or from Spain.
notes.n: More guesswork. The book has not told us where Heathcliff came from.

notes.g: Anyway; in any case.
Telling me to go away at once.
Went back to my spying post.
The servant girl who milked the cows and made butter and cheese.
Outing; trip.
Reasoning with her; gently protesting.

notes.t: they made a distinction between her treatment and mine
notes.g: They treated her very differently from me.
notes.n: Catherine is a gentleman's daughter; Heathcliff is taken for a servant or a vagabond. Class decides everything in this scene.

notes.g: Bowl.
A glass of hot wine mixed with water, sugar and spice.
notes.n: Named after Colonel Francis Negus, who made it popular in the early 1700s. A 'tumbler' is a drinking glass.

notes.g: Staring with his mouth open.
Empty; expressionless.

notes.t: There will more come of this business than you reckon on
notes.g: More will come of this than you expect.
notes.n: 'Reckon on' means count on or expect.

notes.g: Take drastic measures.
Unlucky escapade.
To improve things (said ironically: he made them worse).
The next day.

notes.t: read the young master such a lecture on the road he guided his family
notes.g: Lectured Hindley so sternly about the way he ran his family.

notes.t: stirred to look about him, in earnest
notes.g: Roused to pay serious attention.
Get him thrown out of the house.
notes.n: Like a servant being sacked.

notes.g: Now this means Hindley's wife (Frances), not his mother.
Properly under control.
Using cunning and charm instead of force.
